subject: language_arts

unit.title: Word classes & sentence types
unit.essentialQuestion: What jobs do words do, and how do sentences come in different types?

title: Questions & exclamations (the special marks)
objectives: By the end, I can write a question with a ? and a true exclamation starting What/How.

vocabulary.definition: an asking sentence — your voice goes UP at the end
the special hook that ends every asking sentence
a big-feeling sentence that starts with What or How
the mark that ends an exclamation

emphasize: A question makes your voice go UP — and it always needs the ? hook. Never a full stop on a question.
A TRUE exclamation sentence starts with What or How and ends with ! — a loud statement with a ! is not the Year 2 exclamation form.
Two moves make questions: start with a question word (who/what/where/when/why/how) or flip the order (The sky is blue. → Is the sky blue?).

keyConcepts: question words: who, what, where, when, why, how
misconceptions: ending a question with a full stop (question mark forgotten)
writing a 'loud statement' with ! and calling it an exclamation — the Y2 form must start What/How
thinking a command with ! (Stop!) is an exclamation sentence
hooks: Listen: 'The sky is blue.' — flat. 'Is the sky blue?' — hear it go UP? Your voice already knows the rule.
priorKnowledge: the four sentence types and their marks (Lesson 18)

digital: question-word bank on screen (who, what, where, when, why, how)

plan.goal: Hear the rising voice: statement flat vs question up; child performs the contrast; retrieve the full stop.
plan.note: The child's own voice is the lesson's main tool — get them performing the rise immediately.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'Is the sky blue?' with a clear rise and answers 'a full stop' for the telling sentence.

script.say: Listen to my voice: The sky is blue. Flat. Now: Is the sky blue? — hear it go UP at the end? An asking sentence needs a special hook on the end — a question mark. Let's master it. Your turn to try the rise… and quick check first: what mark ends a normal telling sentence?
script.adaptHints: Exaggerate the flat/rising contrast theatrically. Swap 'the sky is blue' for a fact about the child's favourite topic.

blocks.prompt: Say it flat, then make it fly: first 'The sky is blue.' then 'Is the sky blue?' — voice UP at the end!

stuckProtocol: If the rise doesn't come: say it together twice with a hand gesture lifting on 'blue?', then let the child solo it.

plan.goal: Model the two question moves (question word / flip the order) and the true exclamation form (What/How … !).
plan.note: Two clear recipes, one for each special mark. Anchor them side by side on the board.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say the two ways to start a question and how a true exclamation begins.

script.say: To make a QUESTION, I often start with a question word — who, what, where, when, why, how — or I flip the order: The sky is blue. becomes Is the sky blue? — and I end with a question mark. Now the other special mark. A real EXCLAMATION sentence starts with What or How: The cake is big. becomes What a big cake! It shows a big feeling and ends with an exclamation mark. Asking → question mark. What or How plus a big feeling → exclamation mark.
script.adaptHints: Point at the question-word bank as each word is said. Perform 'What a big cake!' with genuine delight — the feeling is the point.

rows: start with who/what/where/when/why/how — or flip the order
start with What or How + a big feeling

plan.goal: Shared fixing and transforming: repair 'Is it raining.' together, then turn 'The dog is fast.' into 'What a fast dog!'
plan.note: The broken question is deliberately shown — the child is the fixer. Then the exclamation transformation together.
plan.successCriteria: Child swaps the full stop for a ? and co-builds 'What a fast dog!'

script.say: Here's a question I wrote wrong — it ends in a full stop: Is it raining. Yuck! Read it aloud — your voice went up, but my mark didn't! Fix it for me. … Now let's transform together: The dog is fast. Make it burst — start with 'What a…'
script.adaptHints: Let the child physically choose the ? from the bank. For the exclamation, scaffold just the opener 'What a…' and let the child finish.

check.question: Turn 'The dog is fast.' into an exclamation.

wrongAnswers.answer: The dog is fast!
wrongAnswers.why: loud statement — didn't use the What/How opener
wrongAnswers.remedy: That's a statement wearing a !. A true exclamation sentence begins What or How — start it again with 'What a…'

wrongAnswers.answer: What a fast dog. (full stop)
wrongAnswers.why: right form, wrong mark
wrongAnswers.remedy: You built the burst — now let it burst! Which mark shows the big feeling at the end?

plan.goal: Key diagnostic: transform 'The cake is big.' into an exclamation AND write a question about the cake.
plan.note: Two-part check straight from the script. Probe the rising voice on the question after success.
plan.successCriteria: Child produces 'What a big cake!' and a correctly hooked question (e.g. 'Is the cake big?').

script.say: Double challenge! Take: The cake is big. First — turn it into an exclamation. Then — write me a QUESTION about the cake. When you're done, read your question aloud: how does your voice sound?
script.adaptHints: Swap cake for a treat the child loves. Probe after: 'How does your voice sound for the question?' (it goes up).

blocks.prompt: Turn 'The cake is big.' into an exclamation, then write one question about the cake.
blocks.sample: What a big cake! Is the cake big?

check.question: Turn 'The cake is big.' into an exclamation, then write a question about the cake.
check.expectedAnswer: What a big cake! — and e.g. Is the cake big? / Who made the cake?

wrongAnswers.answer: The cake is big! (as the exclamation)
wrongAnswers.why: confusing a loud statement with an exclamation sentence
wrongAnswers.remedy: An exclamation sentence begins What or How — start it again with 'What…'

wrongAnswers.answer: Is the cake big. (question with a full stop)
wrongAnswers.why: question mark forgotten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it aloud — your voice went up, so it needs the ? hook.

plan.goal: Independent writing: two questions (using the word bank) and one What/How exclamation; then interleave spotting.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Watch for: missing ?; exclamations that are really statements with a !.
plan.successCriteria: Child writes two correctly hooked questions and one true What/How exclamation.

script.say: Author time! Write me two questions — the word bank is right there to start you off — and one true exclamation beginning What or How. Read each one aloud when you finish: your voice will check your marks for you.
script.adaptHints: Aim the questions at the child's interests (write a question about dragons, about football). The read-aloud self-check is the habit to build.

stuckProtocol: Name why: end mark, or exclamation form.
Say it aloud together and listen for the rising voice.
ONE hint: 'Start with a question word.'
Re-ask a simpler flip: The dog is wet. → Is the dog wet?
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the two rules; end on a win.
plan.successCriteria: Child says: questions go up and take ?; exclamations start What/How and take !.

script.say: How does a question sound, and how do exclamation sentences start? … Exactly. You heard your voice rise and added the question mark every time — great listening-to-your-writing.
script.adaptHints: If time is tight, take the answer verbally while the confetti moment plays.

practiceBank.skill: choose the right end mark for a question

block.prompt: Which mark ends an ASKING sentence?
block.explain: Asking sentences make your voice go up — and they always end with the question-mark hook.

wrongAnswers.answer: . full stop
wrongAnswers.why: the question-mark-forgotten habit
wrongAnswers.remedy: Full stops are for flat telling sentences. When your voice goes UP, which special hook catches it?

wrongAnswers.answer: ! exclamation mark
wrongAnswers.why: muddles the two special marks
wrongAnswers.remedy: The ! is for bursting feelings. Asking isn't bursting — it's wondering. Which mark is the asking hook?

hints: It's the mark shaped like a little hook.

reteach.say: Three marks, three jobs. Full stop: flat telling. Question mark: asking, voice up. Exclamation mark: bursting feeling. When a sentence ASKS, only the hook will do.

practiceBank.skill: fix a question ending in a full stop

wrongAnswers.why: question mark forgotten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it aloud — where is my shoe… did your voice go up? Up-voice needs the hook. Swap the mark.

wrongAnswers.why: excitement mark on an asking sentence
wrongAnswers.remedy: Are you bursting about the shoe, or ASKING where it is? It starts with 'Where' — a question word. Which mark follows a question?

hints: It starts with the question word 'Where'.

reteach.say: 'Where' at the front is a giant clue — it's one of the six question words: who, what, where, when, why, how. Any sentence starting with one of those is asking, and asking always ends with the hook: Where is my shoe?

block.definition: who, what, where, when, why, how — starters that make a sentence ask (and end with ?)

practiceBank.skill: write a question using a question word

block.prompt: Write one question about a dog. Start with a question word: who, what, where, when, why or how — and don't forget the hook!

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Any real question starting with a question word and ending with ?, e.g. 'Where does the dog sleep?'

wrongAnswers.answer: Why does the dog bark. (full stop)
wrongAnswers.why: question mark forgotten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Lovely question — now read it aloud. Voice up? Then it needs the ? hook at the end.

wrongAnswers.answer: The dog barks a lot. (a statement)
wrongAnswers.why: wrote a telling sentence instead of an asking one
wrongAnswers.remedy: That TELLS me about the dog. To ASK, start with one of the six question words — try 'Why…' or 'Where…'.

hints: Pick a starter: who, what, where, when, why, how.
Read it back — does your voice go up? Then hook it with ?

reteach.say: A question recipe, three steps: pick a question word — say, WHY. Add your wondering — why does the dog bark. Hook it — why does the dog bark? Question word, wondering, hook. Every time.

block.prompt: Which one is a TRUE exclamation sentence?
block.explain: A true exclamation sentence starts with What or How: What a big cake! The first is a loud statement; the last is a command with a !.

wrongAnswers.answer: The cake is big!
wrongAnswers.why: loud statement mistaken for an exclamation — the Y2 form must start What/How
wrongAnswers.remedy: It's shouty, but check the first word — 'The'. True exclamations begin What or How. Which option does?

wrongAnswers.answer: Eat the cake!
wrongAnswers.why: command with a ! called an exclamation
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Eat' is a bossy verb ordering you about — that's a command borrowing a !. Which option starts with What or How?

hints: Check the FIRST word of each.
True exclamations start with What or How.

reteach.say: Three sentences, all ending with ! — but only one is a true exclamation. The secret is the first word: What a big cake! begins with What. A loud statement or a bossy command can borrow the mark, but they can't borrow the What/How opener.

block.prompt: Sentence surgeon! Put the words back in order to make a question — the hook goes last.

wrongAnswers.answer: The sky is blue? Why
wrongAnswers.why: statement order with a floating question word
wrongAnswers.remedy: The question word leads the parade! Which word starts the asking? Put 'Why' at the front and rebuild.

wrongAnswers.answer: Is why the sky blue?
wrongAnswers.why: flip-move and question-word move mixed together
wrongAnswers.remedy: Pick ONE opener. Here the question word 'Why' goes first, then the rest follows: Why is…

hints: The word carrying the ? goes last.

reteach.say: Questions have a marching order: question word first — Why — then the helper — is — then the rest — the sky blue — and the hook rides on the last word. Why is the sky blue? Question word front, hook at the back.

block.prompt: Read this aloud and make your voice go UP at the end: Is it snowing?

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Reads 'Is it snowing?' with a clear rise at the end

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it flat like a statement
wrongAnswers.why: voice not matching the mark
wrongAnswers.remedy: That sounded like telling! The ? at the end is asking your voice to climb. Try again — lift on 'snowing?'

wrongAnswers.answer: shouts it
wrongAnswers.why: confusing loud with rising
wrongAnswers.remedy: Not louder — HIGHER. Like the end of the sentence is floating up. Iiis it snoooowing?

hints: The ? is a little ramp — ride it up.

reteach.say: Your voice is the question detector. Flat means telling; rising means asking. Listen: It is snowing. — flat. Is it snowing? — up! When you write, read your sentence aloud, and if your voice climbs, the hook goes on.

block.caption: flat voice = full stop · rising voice = question mark

practiceBank.skill: transform one statement into both special types

block.prompt: Stretch! Take 'The dog is fast.' — write it as a question AND as a true exclamation.
block.sample: Is the dog fast? How fast the dog is! (or: What a fast dog!)

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A flipped question (Is the dog fast?) and a What/How exclamation (What a fast dog! / How fast the dog is!)

wrongAnswers.answer: The dog is fast! (as the exclamation)
wrongAnswers.why: loud statement, not the What/How form
wrongAnswers.remedy: The words haven't changed — only the mark got louder! Rebuild it starting with 'What a…' or 'How…'.

wrongAnswers.answer: Is the dog fast. (question with a full stop)
wrongAnswers.why: question mark forgotten after a good flip
wrongAnswers.remedy: Perfect flip! Now read it aloud — voice up? Finish the job with the hook.

hints: For the question: flip it — 'Is the dog…'.
For the exclamation: start with 'What a…' or 'How…'.

reteach.say: One statement, two magic spells. Spell one, the flip: The dog is fast → Is the dog fast? Spell two, the burst: start with What or How → What a fast dog! Same idea, two special sentences, two special marks.

practiceBank.skill: explain why a command with ! is not an exclamation sentence

block.prompt: Expert question: 'Stop!' ends with ! — why is it NOT an exclamation sentence?
options: Because it's too short to be a sentence
Because it starts with a bossy verb, not What or How — it's a command
Because it should end with a question mark
block.explain: The type comes from the job and the opener: 'Stop!' bosses with a bossy verb — a command. True exclamation sentences start with What or How.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Because it starts with a bossy verb, not What or How — it's a command

wrongAnswers.answer: It IS an exclamation sentence
wrongAnswers.why: mark/type confusion
wrongAnswers.remedy: The ! only shows feeling. Check the first word — 'stop' is ordering you about. Which type orders? And what do true exclamations start with?

wrongAnswers.answer: Because it's too short to be a sentence
wrongAnswers.why: length mistaken for the reason
wrongAnswers.remedy: Short can still be a sentence! The real clue is the FIRST word. What kind of word is 'stop', and which type starts that way?

hints: The mark shows feeling; the TYPE comes from the first word's job.
What do true exclamation sentences start with?

reteach.say: This is the cleverest idea in the unit, so let's pin it down: the exclamation MARK is a feeling-flag any strong sentence can wave. But the exclamation TYPE has a strict uniform — it must start What or How. Stop! waves the flag but wears a command's uniform: bossy verb first. Flag ≠ uniform.

block.prompt: Grand stretch! Write a tiny interview: THREE questions for your favourite storybook character — three different question words, a hook on each.
block.sample: Where do you live? Why did you climb the beanstalk? How did you escape the giant?

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Three questions, three different question words, each ending with ?

wrongAnswers.answer: one or more questions ending in a full stop
wrongAnswers.why: question mark forgotten in the flow of writing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Interview check! Read each one aloud — every rising voice needs its hook. Which one is missing it?

wrongAnswers.answer: Tell me about your house. (a command, not a question)
wrongAnswers.why: polite command mistaken for a question
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Tell' is a bossy verb — that's a command in disguise! Rebuild it with a question word: 'Where do you…?'

hints: Pick three different starters from: who, what, where, when, why, how.
Read each aloud — voice up, hook on.

reteach.say: Interviewers use the six question words like keys on a keyring: who, what, where, when, why, how. Pick three keys, unlock three questions: Where do you live? Why did you go? How did you escape? Every key opens with a capital and closes with a hook.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave writing, transforming and mark-vs-type items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the question-word bank on screen, then a level-1 item (choose/fix the mark only).
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one self-written question with ? and one true What/How exclamation → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'questions and exclamations'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: end mark, or exclamation form.
Say it aloud together and listen for the rising voice.
ONE hint: 'Start with a question word.'
Re-ask a simpler flip (The dog is wet. → Is the dog wet?), build back.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Point the questions at the learner's world — their pet, favourite character, best game. The read-it-aloud voice check is the habit in every framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable transform; praise the process — 'you read your sentence aloud and let your voice check the mark.'

differentiation.support: Question-word bank (who, what, where, when, why, how) stays on the desk; work on choose-the-mark items before writing whole questions.
differentiation.stretch: Explain why a command with ! (Stop!) is not an exclamation sentence; write both a What… and a How… exclamation for the same idea.

extension: Write a tiny interview — three questions for a favourite character, three different question words, then read it aloud in your best interviewer voice.
assessmentEvidence: Child writes correctly punctuated questions (question word or flip, ending ?) and one true What/How exclamation ending !.
revisitLater: Sentence types feed the writing in Unit 5 (instructions use commands); quick recall of question/exclamation forms in Lesson 25.
